title: Can a Christian Get a Tattoo?
excerpt: Leviticus 19:28 forbids tattoos in a chapter that also forbids mixed fabrics and trimmed beards. How Christians have read the law of Moses, what the New Testament says about the body, and why this is a question of conscience.
body:
A sixteen-year-old wants a small cross on the inside of her wrist for her birthday, and her father has told her no, because the Bible says no. She has found the verse he means and noticed that it sits a few lines below one about mixed fabrics, and she is wearing a cotton and polyester shirt. A young man who came to faith in his twenties has a sleeve of tattoos from before, some of which he now regrets, and he wonders whether the people in his new church see his arms before they see him. A mother whose son died three years ago has his handwriting tattooed over her heart, a line from the last birthday card he wrote her, and she has been told by someone in her Bible study that she broke a commandment written about mourning the dead.

The skeptic has seen this argument and thinks it shows how Christians use the Bible. They quote Leviticus against tattoos, he says, and ignore the rest of Leviticus whenever it suits them. They call it obedience, but it looks more like taste.

He has a point, and it deserves an answer rather than an eye roll. Some Christians do reach for Leviticus 19:28 as if the rest of the chapter weren't there. But the answer to selective reading is better reading, not giving up on the text. Christians have thought hard for a very long time about how the law of Moses applies to them, and that thinking is what this question needs.

The site's page on whether it's a sin [to drink, get a tattoo, or gamble](/help/is-it-a-sin) is a good companion to this essay, and it gives one piece of advice that belongs at the top: "Something permanent, like a tattoo, deserves a season of prayer and counsel before you decide." It also says something every reader should hear before the argument begins: "On either reading, your standing with God rests on Christ, not your skin."

## The Verse and Its Neighbors

Here is the verse in full: "You shall not make any cuts on your body for the dead or tattoo yourselves: I am the LORD" (Leviticus 19:28). It is short, and it seems clear. But a verse lives in a chapter, and this chapter is one of the most remarkable in the Old Testament.

Leviticus 19 opens with God's call to his people to be holy because he is holy, and then lists, in quick succession, dozens of short commands. Honor your parents. Keep the Sabbath. Leave the edges of your field for the poor. Pay a hired worker the same day. Don't curse the deaf or put a stumbling block before the blind. Judge fairly. And at the center of it all: "you shall love your neighbor as yourself: I am the LORD" (Leviticus 19:18). Jesus would later call that the second great commandment.

The same chapter also says, "nor shall you wear a garment of cloth made of two kinds of material" (Leviticus 19:19), and "You shall not round off the hair on your temples or mar the edges of your beard" (Leviticus 19:27). The ban on tattoos sits right beside the beard law, and both sit just after commands against divination and fortune-telling (Leviticus 19:26) and just before the command not to consult mediums (Leviticus 19:31).

The Study Bible's note on [Leviticus 19](/study/bible/leviticus/19) explains the setting: "The practices it forbids were real features of the world around Israel. Cutting the body in grief is attested among Israel's neighbors, and the prophets of Baal gash themselves in 1 Kings 18:28." That scene on Mount Carmel is vivid. The prophets of Baal "cried aloud and cut themselves after their custom with swords and lances, until the blood gushed out upon them" (1 Kings 18:28). Deuteronomy gives the same prohibition with its reason attached: "You are the sons of the LORD your God. You shall not cut yourselves or make any baldness on your foreheads for the dead" (Deuteronomy 14:1). Israel's way of grieving was to be different from the nations' way, because Israel belonged to a different God.

So the verse is not a free-floating rule about ink. It is about marking the body in the rites of the dead and the worship of other gods, in a chapter that sets Israel apart from its neighbors in dozens of visible ways.

## How Christians Have Read the Law

That still leaves the real question, which is the one the sixteen-year-old put to her father with her cotton and polyester shirt. Which of these laws still bind a Christian, and how do we know?

The note on Leviticus 19 calls this "a fair question, and the chapter itself refuses to separate ritual from ethics." Paying a worker on time and not mixing fabrics stand a few verses apart, both signed with "I am the LORD." Christians have answered in more than one way, and the answers matter here.

A long tradition, found in Thomas Aquinas and John Calvin, divides the law of Moses into moral, civil and ceremonial parts. The moral law, such as love of neighbor, honesty and justice, reflects God's character and still binds everyone. The civil law governed Israel as a nation and expired with that nation's government. The ceremonial law, the sacrifices, purity rules and many of the visible signs that set Israel apart, pointed forward to Christ and was fulfilled in him. The Westminster Confession, written in the 1640s and still the doctrinal standard of many Presbyterian churches, sets out this same threefold division in its chapter on the law of God. On this reading, the tattoo law looks a great deal like the beard law and the fabric law: one of the marks that kept Israel visibly distinct from the nations around it, never repeated in the New Testament.

Another approach, held by many Christians today, says that the whole law of Moses was a covenant given to Israel and fulfilled in Christ, and that Christians are bound by its commands as they are taken up and reshaped in the New Testament. Love of neighbor reappears again and again in the apostles' letters. The beard law, the fabric law and the tattoo law do not. On this reading too, the verse doesn't directly govern a Christian's skin.

Some Christians still read the verse differently, and their case deserves to be heard. The help page states it fairly: they "note that the same chapter's bans on theft and on consulting mediums still bind (Leviticus 19:11, 31), and that God still cares how his people mark the bodies they're told to offer him (Romans 12:1); for them it remains a line God drew." That is a serious argument. It refuses to treat the Old Testament as a rulebook to be quietly retired, and it insists that the body matters to God. A Christian who holds it is not a legalist for doing so.

## The Body Is Not Your Own

The New Testament has no tattoo law, but it has a great deal to say about the body, and none of it supports the idea that a Christian's body is simply his own canvas. "Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body" (1 Corinthians 6:19-20).

That passage is often quoted in arguments about tattoos, but its context is sexual immorality, and it cuts in more than one direction. It rules out treating the body as worthless, and it equally rules out treating the body as a billboard for whatever the self wants to announce. It asks what will glorify God in this body. That question applies to a tattoo, but it also applies to how we eat, how we dress, how we spend money on our appearance and how we judge the appearance of others.

Scripture also offers some surprising images. Isaiah, describing the day when God pours out his Spirit, writes of people eager to belong to him: "This one will say, 'I am the LORD's,' another will call on the name of Jacob, and another will write on his hand, 'The LORD's,' and name himself by the name of Israel" (Isaiah 44:5). Commentators differ on whether a physical mark is meant, and no one should build a doctrine of tattoos on the verse. But it does show that in Scripture a mark on the hand can be a sign of belonging rather than rebellion. Paul wrote, "From now on let no one cause me trouble, for I bear on my body the marks of Jesus" (Galatians 6:17), meaning the scars of his beatings, not ink. And John's vision of the returning Christ includes this detail: "On his robe and on his thigh he has a name written, King of kings and Lord of lords" (Revelation 19:16).

Christians in some parts of the world have long used tattoos to mark their faith. Many Coptic Christians in Egypt have a small cross tattooed on the inside of the wrist, often in childhood, a sign that in some times and places has marked them as Christians in a society where that carried a cost. Pilgrims to Jerusalem have for generations been tattooed there as a record of their pilgrimage. These practices don't settle the question, but they do show that the idea of a Christian tattoo is not a modern invention by people looking for an excuse.

## A Question of Conscience

So where does that leave the father and his daughter? It leaves them in the territory Paul describes in Romans 14, where believers disagreed about food and holy days, and where Paul refused to settle the matter by decree. "Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind" (Romans 14:5). "Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? It is before his own master that he stands or falls" (Romans 14:4). The note on [Romans 14](/study/bible/romans/14) summarizes the chapter: "Those whose faith allows them to eat anything must not look down on those who abstain, and those who abstain must not condemn those who eat." The essay on [whether Christians should drink](/writing/should-christians-drink-alcohol) reads that chapter at length.

Whether a Christian may get a tattoo is a question of the third order, the kind on which faithful believers have reached different answers without either side abandoning the faith. Scripture doesn't settle it with a clear New Testament command, and this essay won't pretend to settle it either. It can say what the question involves.

Conscience matters. Paul is blunt: "For whatever does not proceed from faith is sin" (Romans 14:23). A Christian who believes a tattoo is wrong and gets one anyway has done wrong, whatever the verse originally meant.

Motives matter. Jesus taught that what defiles a person comes from within, and the help page quotes him at length on that point. A tattoo meant to honor God or remember a loved one is a different thing from one meant to provoke, to shock, or to declare that no one can tell you what to do. The Lord "sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). That cuts against vanity, and it cuts against judging others by their skin.

Permanence matters. Ink is hard to take back. That isn't a sin, but it is a reason for patience, prayer and the counsel of people who know you. Many tattoos chosen at eighteen look different at forty.

Other people matter. The young person who lives at home owes real weight to the parents' answer. The help page puts it simply: "If you're young and live at home, your parents' answer carries weight." Paul's rule for the strong was to care about the weak: "For you were called to freedom, brothers. Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another" (Galatians 5:13). And over all of it: "So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God" (1 Corinthians 10:31).

## What We Have Made of It

The church's trouble with this question has not usually been bad exegesis. It has been the way we treat people. Many of us have judged a stranger by his sleeves before we knew his name. We have let a young man with tattoos from his old life feel like he had to wear long sleeves to be welcome, as though grace stopped at the skin. We have told grieving mothers that their mourning was disobedient, using a verse about pagan funeral rites against a woman whose only rite was love. And we have sometimes, in the other direction, treated a tattoo as a badge of being relaxed and modern, a way of signaling that we're not like those other Christians, which is its own kind of vanity.

The skeptic was right that Christians often read Leviticus selectively. He was wrong if he thought the only alternatives were reading it woodenly or not reading it at all. The church has a long and careful tradition of reading it in the light of Christ. When we abandon that tradition in favor of whatever rule feels right, we deserve his criticism.

## Marked by Another

The deepest Christian answer to the question of marks on the body isn't about ink. It's about scars. After his resurrection, Jesus showed his disciples his hands and his side (John 20:20), and to Thomas he said, "Put your finger here, and see my hands" (John 20:27). The risen Christ still carries marks on his body, and they are the marks of his love for people who did not deserve it. Christians belong to him not because of anything written on their skin, but because of what was written on his.

The sixteen-year-old and her father may still disagree after reading all of this, and that is allowed. What they shouldn't do is treat the disagreement as a test of faith. The young man in the new church can stop wondering whether his arms disqualify him; they don't. And the mother with her son's handwriting over her heart was not cutting herself before a foreign god, as the prophets of Baal did on Carmel. Whatever she concludes about the verse, she was grieving, and the God who keeps count of our tossings and puts our tears in his bottle (Psalm 56:8) sees what she wrote and why.

*"Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price."* (1 Corinthians 6:19-20)

*"So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God."* (1 Corinthians 10:31)
